A part of me suspects that Steam Machines were, in part, created to act as a showcase for Vulkan. Although Linux gaming is possible, most desktops with Linux on them are not gaming rigs. By creating what is, in effect, a Linux gaming console, Valve has created a ready test bench to see what Vulkan can do.

It is going to be an interesting few years.

It's relatively common to see companies make a profit from their free (both libre and gratis) software by packaging it pre-installed on hardware. I imagine that was the reason SteamOS got the greenlight in the first place. They likely stand to make more from this than selling games they wouldn't otherwise sell without giving devs a target platform for their GNU/Linux ports.
It more than likely got the go ahead because Valve knew that Windows Store is a nearly direct competitor to Steam and probably could become a valid way for companies to distribute games.
